reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Characterised by excessive downward ballooning of the perineum during straining, reflecting a weak, lax pelvic floor
Typically follows years of chronic straining at stool and is associated with obstructed defecation, mucosal prolapse, and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome
Presents with incomplete evacuation, a sensation of a lump or perineal bulging, mucus discharge, and progressive faecal incontinence as a pudendal neuropathy develops
Clinically the perineum descends below the plane of the ischial tuberosities on straining, which a perineometer or defecography can quantify
Chronic descent stretches the pudendal nerves, producing a neuropathy that leads to sphincter weakness and incontinence over time
Management is largely conservative: avoiding straining, treating constipation, and pelvic floor physiotherapy or biofeedback; surgery has a limited and unreliable role
It forms part of the spectrum of pelvic floor weakness and often coexists with pelvic organ prolapse
reference.pathophysiology: Descending perineum syndrome results from chronic excessive straining that progressively weakens and stretches the pelvic floor, so that on defecatory effort the perineum balloons abnormally downward. The prolapsing anterior rectal mucosa produces a sensation of obstruction, provoking further straining in a vicious cycle. Sustained descent stretches the pudendal nerves as they course around the ischial spines, causing a progressive pudendal neuropathy with denervation of the sphincter and pelvic floor and eventual faecal incontinence. It overlaps with mucosal prolapse and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructed defecation syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of perineal descent on straining, aided by a perineometer
Defecography (fluoroscopic or MR) to quantify descent and demonstrate prolapse
Anorectal manometry to assess sphincter pressures
Pudendal nerve terminal motor latency or neurophysiology where incontinence is present
Endoanal ultrasound to assess sphincter integrity
Colonic transit and balloon expulsion where evacuatory dysfunction is assessed
redFlags: Progressive faecal incontinence indicating an advancing pudendal neuropathy
New bleeding, weight loss, or a mass suggesting malignancy
Rapidly progressive symptoms or neurological signs suggesting a spinal cause
Ulceration with atypical features requiring biopsy
reference.prognosis: Generally a chronic, slowly progressive condition; established pudendal neuropathy and incontinence are difficult to reverse, so prevention through avoiding straining and early conservative management is important, and surgical results are inconsistent.
pitfalls: Attempting surgery with the expectation of a reliable cure
Overlooking the underlying straining or evacuatory disorder
Missing early pudendal neuropathy before incontinence is established
Failing to address coexisting pelvic organ prolapse
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Keighley & Williams' Surgery of the Anus, Rectum and Colon
management: Correct the underlying constipation and eliminate straining with increased dietary fibre and fluids, osmotic or bulk-forming laxatives, and toileting retraining to abolish prolonged defecatory effort
Pelvic floor physiotherapy with biofeedback to restore coordinated evacuation and support the lax pelvic floor
Treat coexisting mucosal prolapse and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome and discourage digitation and repeated straining
Barrier skin care for perineal soreness and mucus discharge, with antimotility agents such as loperamide for associated faecal incontinence
Serial anorectal physiology and defecographic surveillance for progressive pudendal neuropathy and worsening continence
Consider sacral neuromodulation for established faecal incontinence, and reserve surgery such as rectopexy for selected refractory cases given its inconsistent results
Manage within a colorectal and pelvic floor multidisciplinary team, escalating specialist assessment if evacuatory failure or incontinence progresses
